Raúl Zuleta
← Back to projects ESEN

How can we come to know an environment without ceasing to inhabit it?

Viejito-Perro began during the holidays following my candidacy examination. I wanted to put my computing skills into practice and enjoy learning something new, so I decided to repurpose an old laptop as a home server. I first installed services that could be useful within the household, then added development boards and environmental sensors. As the system began to record and compare what was happening in different parts of the home, questions emerged that had not been fully formulated at the outset.

The project became a way of exploring a concern that had arisen during the first year of my PhD: the gap between lived experience and measured data. Models, averages and representations allow us to know the world, while also potentially distancing us from its sensory experience.

Viejito-Perro traces how an environmental variation becomes a signal, a datum, a comparison and an interpretation. Measurements are not treated as transparent representations. They depend on where sensors are placed, on technical decisions and on the everyday practices through which they acquire context.

The project does not seek to resolve the distance between knowing and inhabiting. It explores whether an infrastructure for measurement can heighten attention to the environment, while also asking how that infrastructure might technologise or simplify our experience of it.

Relationship to my trajectory

From observing mediations to building them

The project extends several practices from my anthropological training: situated observation, archive building, attention to events and failures, and the reflexive examination of instruments, data and infrastructures. My additional training enabled me to bring these concerns into the construction and testing of a material system.

Viejito-Perro is an independent project developed during my PhD. It shares with my doctoral research an interest in instruments and in translations between matter and information, but it is not part of the thesis’s ethnographic field and does not constitute one of its findings.

An old computer takes on a new form

The computer that gave rise to the project was passed on to me after many years of use. When I received it to play and experiment with, its age brought to mind the saying “you can’t teach an old dog new tricks”.

The name acknowledges the time, care and affection invested in extending its life by giving it new capabilities. Several decisions, including its lighting behaviours and the character incorporated into the screen, arose from a desire to share the project’s development with others in an approachable way.

Acto de Amor thus names a way of building grounded in care, reuse and the involvement of others.

Drawing on the illustration and the first sketch, I developed a parametric casing model for node 02 in OpenSCAD. Its first physical print will make it possible to test dimensions, ventilation, access to components and the strength of the assembly.

How it works

The sensors record selected variations in the living room and bedroom. Two nodes gather the readings and send them to a local server, where they are stored and compared. A screen, lights and graphical interfaces express some of the relationships among them.

  1. The environment varies
  2. The sensors record
  3. Nodes gather and transmit
  4. The local server stores and compares
  5. Interfaces express relationships

At each step, a variation within the home is transformed: first into a signal, then into a record, a comparison and a form of expression.

Domestic infrastructure

A repurposed computer acts as a server. Two nodes connected to the local network gather and transmit readings from the living room and bedroom.

Environmental records

The system records temperature, humidity, pressure and light levels. Particle readings and acoustic activity remain experimental.

Acoustic activity is converted locally into relative indicators: no audio recordings are transmitted or stored.

Archive and comparison

Measurements are stored within the home to build a historical archive, compare rooms and relate them to outdoor reference data.

A form that emerges through building

Viejito-Perro was not designed all at once. Its form has emerged through successive additions, tests, failures and new questions. Each added capacity—to record, compare, store or express—changes the system and brings different aspects of the home into view.

Failures also create opportunities for learning. A sensor that stops responding, a reading affected by the device’s position or an inadequate outdoor comparison reveals the conditions required to produce and interpret data.

What the archive began to reveal

The accumulated archive showed that the nodes do not simply describe a living room and a bedroom. Each records a specific material position shaped by light, proximity to windows, air circulation, everyday activities and the assembly itself.

Environmental cycles

They appear in daily patterns of light, warming and cooling.

Domestic rhythms

They become visible through recurring differences in acoustic activity, temperature and humidity.

Brief events

Cooking or ventilation can produce marked variations that disappear when data are summarised as hourly averages.

These differences do not automatically reveal what happened. An increase in humidity does not in itself indicate a shower, and silence does not prove that a room is empty. Interpreting the measurements requires relating them to observations, notes and situated knowledge of the home.

Interfaces in operation

Status and limits

Viejito-Perro is operational, but it is neither a finished product nor a calibrated scientific instrument. The system makes it possible to observe partial relationships and formulate questions; it does not provide a complete or neutral representation of the environment.

  • Readings depend on location and mounting.
  • Acoustic indicators are not equivalent to measurements calibrated in decibels.
  • The outdoor references are regional and modelled.
  • Interpretations of domestic activities remain contextualised hypotheses.

Open lines

  • Evaluate and adjust the first casing currently being printed.
  • Install and calibrate LD2410C presence sensors on both nodes to distinguish more clearly among presence, movement and absence.
  • Investigate forms of autonomous communication between them.
  • Develop visual, sonic and historical ways of engaging with the records.

Authorship and collaborations

My work

I defined the project’s concept and principles, reconditioned and managed the server, selected and assembled the components, carried out the physical tests, designed behaviours and interfaces, contextualised the measurements, and directed the project’s development and documentation.

AI assistance

Some code, configurations and documentation were developed iteratively with assistance from AI tools, under my direction, review and testing on the physical system.

Constanza Tizzoni

The original drawing of the character and the first visual explorations of its casing were created by Constanza Tizzoni. The screen bitmap and subsequent 3D models derive from that drawing and are published with her permission.

Nicolás Müller

He has been my main technical interlocutor in the laboratory. We have spoken frequently about sensors, connections, electronics and fabrication. He has helped me solve assembly and soldering problems, reviewed the casing model, and provided access to the laboratory’s 3D printer, which we are currently using to produce its first physical version.

Alejandro Bustos

He has contributed through conversations about the project’s direction and possibilities. Drawing on his experience with electronics, he has helped me clarify decisions and open up new lines of exploration. He also gave me a sensor that has not yet been incorporated into the system.

Problem

Process

My contribution

Collaboration and credits

Evidence and materials

    The teaching challenge

    The project addressed a difficulty that became apparent in 2023. A participatory assessment conducted with students revealed uncertainty about how to evaluate the impact of interventions undertaken during their professional placements. Together with subsequent reflection among teaching staff, this drew attention to a gap: students could administer instruments and calculate results, giving them a basis for evaluating their interventions, but they needed further guidance in scoring and interpreting those instruments and turning the results into context-sensitive diagnoses that could inform decisions in schools.

    Against this background, I began developing the idea of a support system that would connect technical operations with professional reasoning. The proposal took shape in 2026 through collective work at CIPSE.

    From questionnaire to pedagogical system

    The starting point was the Cuestionario de Convivencia Escolar para la No Violencia (School Coexistence Questionnaire for Non-Violence), developed and psychometrically validated by Flavio Muñoz Troncoso, Sandra Becerra Peña and Enrique Riquelme. From the students’ perspective, the instrument jointly examines different forms of school violence and aspects of how school coexistence is managed institutionally.

    On this basis, a system comprising four elements was developed:

    • a teaching manual for administration, scoring and interpretation;
    • a software application for processing, reviewing and visualising data;
    • an initial training session;
    • and guidance while preparing the diagnosis and recommendations for intervention.

    The application reduced part of the operational workload and organised results by factors and dimensions. It also generated visualisations and preliminary interpretations. These outputs did not replace professional judgement: they had to be reviewed in light of the school context, data quality and other sources of information.

    A four-week pilot

    The system was piloted for four weeks with seventeen fifth-year Psychology students working in pairs and undertaking placements in schools in the Coquimbo Region.

    The process included initial training, administration of the instrument, technical and interpretive guidance sessions, preparation of diagnostic reports, and reporting the findings back to the schools.

    I also took part in a guidance session focused on interpreting results and designing intervention strategies. We worked on reading and interpreting statistics and on moving from results organised by the application to contextualised diagnoses and recommendations that schools could use.

    Diagnostic reports, usability and satisfaction questionnaires, and exit interviews were collected. When I left CIPSE and Universidad Central de Chile in August 2026, these materials had not yet been fully analysed. I do not know whether the analysis continued afterwards.

    The experience therefore establishes that the system was designed, implemented and evaluated in an authentic educational setting. It does not yet demonstrate its effectiveness in strengthening diagnostic skills.

    Learning to work across disciplines

    Developing the application required translating psychological and pedagogical criteria into processing rules, data structures and interface decisions. This translation involved revisiting concepts, specifying procedures and deciding which operations could be automated and which needed to remain open to interpretation.

    The collaboration provided a concrete example of interdisciplinary work. Computing reduced repetitive operations and made certain relationships among the results visible, while educational psychology provided the criteria required to interpret those results without separating them from their context.

    The project showed that automating calculations is not the same as automating diagnosis. The application could organise information and propose preliminary interpretations, but students still had to review the data, relate them to other sources, and justify their interpretations and recommendations.

    My contribution

    The 2023 participatory assessment identified the initial problem. Building on those findings, I formulated the proposal for the system, selected CENVI as its foundational instrument, and coordinated its pedagogical development while serving as director of CIPSE.

    My work on the manual centred on editing and coordination. I wrote the introduction and established the document’s overall tone, seeking to keep its technical guidance connected to diagnostic reasoning and context-sensitive decision-making.

    I also defined criteria for interpretation and ongoing guidance, coordinated the project’s psychological and pedagogical requirements with the software-development team, took part in the pilot, and contributed to the design and administration of its evaluation instruments. I also prepared the project’s institutional presentation and a conference abstract.

    Collaboration and credits

    Jorge Mavrakis, a student member of CIPSE, and Matías Barraza, an external collaborator whom Jorge invited to join the project, jointly developed the software application in dialogue with the project’s psychological and pedagogical requirements. Jorge also designed and delivered training on its use and supported part of the implementation.

    Tania Guerrero, the course instructor, integrated the system into the students’ field placements and participated in its implementation.

    The project was developed collectively at CIPSE-UCEN. The Cuestionario de Convivencia Escolar para la No Violencia was developed and psychometrically validated by Flavio Muñoz Troncoso, Sandra Becerra Peña and Enrique Riquelme.

    From a shared need to a system of documents

    The project grew out of a consultation process conducted in 2018. Through conversations, workshops and working sessions, I gathered the views and needs of people involved in school coexistence. The process culminated in a municipality-wide meeting held on 11 December that year.

    The findings showed a need for clearer municipal guidance and for tools that could translate the general aims of school coexistence into concrete ways of organising work.

    My supervisor asked me to prepare what the institution called a Política Comunal de Convivencia Escolar (Municipal School Coexistence Policy). During 2019, I transformed these findings, together with regulations and ministerial documents, into an interconnected set of materials. The completed proposal was presented to the mayor, approved by municipal decree and subsequently presented to the municipal education community.

    The central document defined objectives, conceptual foundations, levels of intervention and a multi-year programme. Alongside it, I developed five complementary guidance documents covering:

    • the preparation of the Plan de Gestión de la Convivencia Escolar;
    • the formation and management of school coexistence teams;
    • support for teachers to strengthen classroom interactions;
    • strengthening the role of form teachers;
    • role profiles for school coexistence coordinators and two-person psychosocial teams.

    Together, these materials sought to translate national regulations and the general aims of school coexistence into roles, procedures and tools that could be used in everyday practice.

    Documents to organise practices

    The guidance documents included cycles of assessment, planning, monitoring and evaluation; matrices for developing plans; competency profiles; classroom observation and teacher feedback forms; learning indicators; materials for working with families; and an adaptation of agile methods for coordinating the teams’ work.

    The documents sought to establish a shared way of organising work, distributing responsibilities, making progress visible, keeping records and linking the activities of each school to municipality-wide objectives.

    The guidance was not intended to replace the autonomy of school communities. It offered a shared language and structure within which each school could make its own decisions.

    Presentation and circulation

    The completed policy and its supplementary documents were presented in 2019 at a municipality-wide meeting where members of the Department of Education presented our work plans to teachers from municipal schools.

    The materials were officially distributed to the schools. I coordinated the production of multiple copies and personally placed printed sets in the correspondence slots used by each school.

    My contribution

    I was responsible for writing, structuring and laying out the central document and the five complementary guidance documents, as well as designing their instruments.

    The work included reviewing regulations, ministerial documents and relevant literature; defining the conceptual framework; organising the system of documents; and creating diagrams, matrices, role profiles, forms and working tools.

    I also arranged the presentation of the proposal to the mayor, participated in its institutional formalisation, presented the project to the teaching community, and coordinated the reproduction and distribution of the materials.

    Forms designed to record classroom observations and guide feedback to teachers.

    Implementation and limits

    Implementation fell short of what had been planned. I found it difficult to sustain a monitoring system that would show how each school was using the documents, provide support when difficulties arose, and allow the guidance to be adjusted in a timely manner.

    Some practices nevertheless remained in place, including the preparation of management plans using the format proposed by the policy and the monthly monitoring procedures it established.

    The proposal was not understood or taken up in the same way by everyone involved. This was particularly evident in one-teacher rural schools, whose organisation, staffing and working conditions did not match several of the organisational assumptions built into the documents.

    The initial participatory process helped identify needs and establish a point of departure, but it did not by itself ensure later uptake. Gaps remained between gathering input, producing documents and transforming institutional practices, and the project was not able to bridge them completely.

    In retrospect, the experience demonstrates both the capacity to build an institutional architecture and the limits of trying to coordinate heterogeneous school realities through general guidance. Designing, approving and distributing documents does not guarantee that they will become sustained practices.

    Relationship to my trajectory

    This experience shifted my attention from individual interpretations towards public policies, organisations and the instruments used to coordinate work at a distance.

    Daily engagement with regulations, indicators, guidance documents and a diverse range of schools later influenced my decision to study sociology and conduct a historical analysis of the Política Nacional de Convivencia Escolar. That research was not the original basis of the municipal project, but it revisited questions that had become visible through this professional experience.

    Currency of the documents

    This page presents excerpts from the central document and the five guidance documents, including planning diagrams, competency matrices, and observation and feedback forms.

    The documents were prepared in 2019 using the regulations, policies and references then in force. They are presented as historical evidence of professional and institutional work, not as up-to-date guidance for schools.

    Building a representation of the experience

    The team collectively developed a user profile, an empathy map, a journey map and a service blueprint. These tools helped us organise the available information and represent the experience of requesting a cash advance before, during and after the service.

    The analysis focused on three problems identified through the professional experience of the team member who worked at Cencosud:

    • the lack of updated financial information;
    • the risk of missing payments because reminders were not received in time;
    • difficulty understanding and comparing financing options.

    Based on these problems, the team defined three principles to guide the proposal: security and reliability, accessibility and ease of use, and financial education.

    The journey map and service blueprint were working tools created to organise the case and develop a proposal within the diploma programme.

    Translating the proposal into an interface

    Open the design file in Figma ↗

    The proposal brought together three main components:

    • a flow for simulating a cash-advance request and reviewing the breakdown of its costs;
    • a visualisation of monthly spending;
    • a payment-reminder system showing the potential interest savings associated with paying on time.

    The screens sought to organise complex financial information through visual hierarchies, charts, notices and sequences that were easy to understand.

    The result was a non-navigable set of screens designed in Figma. The file retains different variants and stages of the work, as well as the screens selected for the final presentation.

    My contribution

    I took part in the collective analysis of the experience, the development of the working tools and the overall definition of the proposal. I then assumed full responsibility for translating those decisions into the redesigned interface.

    I created every screen presented in the project, including their visual composition, information hierarchy, graphical representation of spending and costs, and the organisation of the different stages of the experience.

    When the project began, I did not know how to use Figma. My previous experience with vector-editing software helped me recognise some principles of graphic construction, but I learned the new tool through tutorials and direct experimentation. The need to materialise the proposal gave this technical learning a specific purpose and context.

    Relationship to my trajectory

    This exercise occupies a limited, specific place within my trajectory. It allowed me to turn previous experience with visual-editing tools into a practice of interface design and to learn Figma through a concrete problem.

    Its inclusion in the portfolio documents that experience of translating between analysis, representation and prototyping. The financial case was the particular setting in which this learning took place and did not define a subsequent line of work.

    Collaboration and credits

    The project was developed jointly by Pablo Poblete, Wendy Vazquez, Benjamín Gallegos, Pablo Pincheira and Raúl Zuleta. The analysis of the experience, the development of the working tools and the overall definition of the proposal were collective.

    I was solely responsible for redesigning the application and creating all its screens in Figma.

    Scope and limits

    During development, we showed the proposal to people known to members of the team and gathered their impressions. This informal review helped us discuss whether the screens were understandable and how the information could be presented more clearly. It did not involve actual Cencosud users.

    The persona named “Miguel”, his characteristics and the quotations included in the presentation were created for the exercise. The names, amounts, transactions, dates and calculations shown on the screens are also simulated. The project used neither personal financial data nor information belonging to real users.

    Although the problem was introduced by a team member who worked at Cencosud, the proposal was not commissioned, institutionally tested or approved by Cencosud Scotiabank. It should be understood as an academic exercise in analysis, design and prototyping.

    A domestic plant-observation system

    What does it take for a set of plants grown at home to become an object of observation?

    The project brings together domestic cultivation, daily photographs, environmental and substrate sensors, practices of care, logs and a data archive. Its purpose is not to conduct a controlled biological experiment, but to observe how plants, instruments, records and everyday decisions jointly come to constitute an object of knowledge.

    It began with tomatoes, radishes and basil being sown in two germination trays. During the first few days, observation depended primarily on photographs and sensory judgements such as the appearance of the substrate, its moisture to the touch and the visible emergence of each species.

    Building something that can be followed

    It soon became clear that producing a comparable series required creating conditions for continuity. The trays were labelled and placed within markings that allowed them to be returned to approximately the same position. An arrow recorded their orientation relative to the window, while a map linked each cell to an identifier.

    Daily photography documented emergence and early growth. The radishes were the first to appear, followed by the basil and tomatoes. Comparing the images, however, was not automatic: the camera angle, time of day, lighting, position of the trays and processing of the files all changed what could be seen.

    The observational setup did not precede the cultivation. It took shape alongside the plants as new needs for identification, comparison and recording emerged.

    1 / 20

    Variations in framing, lighting and setup form part of the record: the sequence has not been aligned or standardised.

    From sensory judgement to instrumental signals

    The decision to water began as a practical assessment of the substrate: looking at its colour, touching it and deciding whether it still retained moisture. A plant node was subsequently added, comprising two capacitive substrate sensors, a light sensor and a sensor measuring temperature, ambient humidity and pressure.

    The sensors do not replace sensory observation, nor do they directly describe the condition of the plants. Each reading depends on the position and depth of the sensor, its wiring and power supply, and the configuration of the assembly.

    The substrate probes currently produce raw voltage values. These make it possible to track variation, but do not yet correspond to calibrated moisture percentages. Keeping them in their original units avoids presenting an interpretation as though it were a direct and definitive measurement.

    A node connected to Viejito-Perro

    Plant Node 01 is technically integrated with Viejito-Perro’s domestic infrastructure. The node collects readings, Home Assistant is used to monitor its operation, and a separate service stores a snapshot of six variables every minute.

    The archive separates automated telemetry from human observations and events. Watering, photographs, movements, thinning, sensor changes and calibrations are recorded as distinct events. This separation makes it possible to relate an instrumental variation to what occurred around the plants without reducing either to the other.

    Huerto is an independent project. It uses part of Viejito-Perro’s infrastructure but develops its own question, protocol and archive.

    1. Cultivationgrowth and events
    2. Sensorssituated signals
    3. Plant nodereading and transmission
    4. Local archivetelemetry and events kept separate

    Sustaining life also transforms what is observed

    Observing the cultivation requires practices that sustain the plants’ lives. Watering, providing light, thinning, transplanting and responding to visible changes are not external to the observational setup: they maintain the conditions that make both plant growth and continued observation possible.

    Nor do these practices preserve an unchanging object. Each intervention alters the subsequent trajectories of the cultivation and what can be recorded. Care sustains life, but it also selects, directs and transforms its possibilities.

    During the first thinning of the radishes, different criteria were applied in two cells. In one, the larger plant was retained; in the other, the smaller one. The removed seedlings were photographed and weighed, partially incorporating a phenotyping practice encountered during fieldwork.

    The procedure does not constitute a comparative experiment, nor does it reproduce a complete laboratory protocol. Its importance lies in showing how a conversation, a tool and a decision about care can introduce new operations of observation into a domestic setting.

    The continuity of the archive

    Distributed care

    The continuity of the plants, the cultivation and its records has depended neither exclusively on one person nor solely on the automatic operation of the sensors. During an absence, another person in the household maintained the watering and produced part of the photographic record, following general instructions on framing and orientation.

    Circulating one photograph through a messaging platform reduced its resolution and removed some original metadata. The episode showed that provenance and comparability also depend on people, instructions, devices and platforms.

    Correcting without erasing

    During the first few days, the positions of the two substrate probes were documented incorrectly. Comparison of the series showed that the behaviour of each channel was more consistent with the opposite assignment.

    The correction did not modify the historical values or swap the sensors’ electrical names. The annotation linking each channel to its physical position was corrected, and the error was preserved as part of the archive’s history.

    Relationship to the doctoral research

    Huerto is an independent material exploration developed during my PhD. It is not part of the fieldwork, does not use ethnographic data from the thesis and is not one of its findings.

    It shares with the doctoral research questions about the operations through which living organisms are identified, fragmented, measured and converted into information. Some practices incorporated into the project were learned or suggested during fieldwork, but transferring them to a domestic setting produced a different setup, with its own purposes and conditions.

    The project makes it possible to experiment on a small scale with relationships between care, measurement, archiving and knowledge, without presenting the home as equivalent to a laboratory or the cultivation as a controlled experiment.

    Current status

    An ongoing cultivation and an open archive

    As of 10 October 2026

    The cultivation remains active and the photographic series extends to day 23 after sowing. On 3 October the tomatoes were thinned, two radishes were extracted and measured, and the other two were transplanted into individual pots. The retained tomatoes continued to grow and their transplant was being prepared; thinning the basil remained pending.

    The node and data archive remain operational. The substrate probes still require situated calibration, and the cultivation cycle is ongoing.

    Limits

    • It is not a controlled biological experiment, and the plants do not function as comparable replicas.
    • The raw probe voltages do not yet correspond to moisture percentages.
    • Photographic conditions are not entirely constant.
    • The series can trace temporal associations but cannot establish causal relationships.
    • Practices transferred from the laboratory are anonymised and do not represent complete protocols.
    • Automated infrastructure does not replace human decisions about observation and care.

    Authorship and collaboration

    My work

    I conceptualised and designed the project, carried out the planting and daily care, built the plant node, defined the observation protocol, configured the data archive, and prepared and interpreted the logs.

    Distributed care

    Another person in the household temporarily helped with watering and taking photographs, allowing the cultivation to continue during my absence.

    Fieldwork exchanges and technical assistance

    Some components and practices emerged from exchanges during fieldwork. These contributions remain anonymised to protect the people and spaces involved. Programming, configuration and technical review have also received support from artificial intelligence tools under my direction and verification.

    Pieces 01 Metagenome 02 Retrato familiar

    01 · Experimental sound practice

    Metagenome

    A sound exploration inspired by Alien Ocean

    17 May 2025 · 2 min 55 s

    Listen to the piece

    Metagenome

    Performance, composition and editing by Raúl Zuleta.

    Work published on a non-commercial basis. An AIFF master is retained and a compressed copy is used for web playback.

    Listening to a community that does not form a single organism

    Metagenome emerged during the first year of my PhD from reading Stefan Helmreich’s Alien Ocean and from a conversation about post-qualitative research methods. The piece explores what the book’s conceptual and affective atmosphere might sound like: an ocean populated by microbial forms of life, technologies of observation and unstable boundaries between the human and the non-human.

    It does not seek to represent a metagenome scientifically or to convert biological data into sound. It is a material exploration developed through sound-making, listening and editing.

    A metagenome brings together the genetic material of an entire microbial community within an environment. It does not refer to an isolated organism, but to multiple forms of life that coexist and interact.

    This idea guided the construction of the piece. Rather than seeking a central melody or dominant voice, I worked with layers, textures and sounds capable of suggesting a medium populated by simultaneous presences. The ocean appears as a fluid, mutable environment: a network in which organisms, signals and material conditions transform together.

    The initial image was a glass of seawater understood as an ecosystem and a living sensor in which signals from a changing world are inscribed.

    Building through improvisation and iteration

    To create the piece, I obtained a MIDI controller and drew on my previous experience of playing music as an amateur.

    The process began with a sonic intention: to produce a long, sustained note. I sat in front of the controller and computer, tried different virtual instruments and continued searching until I found a sound that approached that initial image.

    From there, I alternated between two operations. On the one hand, I performed different tracks from scratch using the MIDI controller and GarageBand’s virtual instruments. On the other, I searched Freesound for recordings that could introduce atmospheres, movements and presences that were difficult to produce with the controller alone.

    Each sound I incorporated changed what the piece seemed to need next. The composition emerged through improvisation, listening, selection, repetition, layering and editing.

    Deciding that a piece is finished

    One of the main difficulties was not beginning the piece but deciding when to stop. The working structure allowed me to continue adding layers, replacing sounds and modifying relationships almost indefinitely.

    Considering it finished required recognising that the piece had reached a form capable of sustaining the exploration, even though other possibilities remained open. Bringing it to a close meant provisionally accepting the form that had emerged.

    Materials and editing

    The piece combines four tracks performed with a MIDI controller and five sounds sourced from Freesound. Editing and production were carried out in GarageBand.

    The instrumental tracks were performed from scratch. The external sounds were trimmed, arranged and combined within the composition to create a marine and more-than-human atmosphere.

    The final version is 2 minutes and 55 seconds long.

    Relationship to my doctoral research

    Metagenome was created during my doctoral studies and arose from a reading connected to my training in the anthropology of science.

    The piece is a parallel exploration of other ways of thinking with concepts, materials and atmospheres. Rather than analysing the book exclusively through writing, it engages with some of its images and problems through listening, sound-making and editing.

    Authorship and credits

    I conceived, performed, composed and edited the piece. I performed the four instrumental tracks using a MIDI controller and GarageBand’s virtual instruments.

    The composition incorporates the following sounds from Freesound.

    • “09347 sinking in the sea.wav”, by Robinhood76 — CC BY-NC 4.0.
    • “Dive Deep preview.mp3”, by hisoul — CC BY 4.0.
    • “205015__xserra__ocean_hpsModel_result.wav”, published by Ave_Rapina — CC0.
    • “Sea Ambience.wav”, by markj_visuals — CC0.
    • “Breathing – Slow, Distraught, Tired”, by TomchikRec — CC BY 4.0.

    The work is published on a non-commercial basis and in accordance with the attribution requirements of the materials used.

    Scope

    Metagenome is an experimental sound practice, not a sonification of data or a scientific representation of microbial communities. Nor does it seek to faithfully reproduce the argument of Alien Ocean.

    Its scope is much more modest: to explore what I can do when I attempt to extend an anthropological reading through instruments, found sounds, improvisation and editing.

    02 · Collaborative sound practice in development

    Retrato familiar

    A sound montage centred on a canto a lo divino singer

    In development since May–June 2026 · 5 min 40 s draft

    Listen to the draft

    Retrato familiar

    Advanced draft, approximately sixty per cent complete.

    The structure and conceptual direction are defined, but additional recordings are needed to complete the ending and produce the final mix.

    A portrait built solely with sounds

    Retrato familiar is a sound montage constructed from Javiera Montecinos’s field archive on canto a lo divino, a Chilean tradition of sung religious poetry. The piece centres on Don Gilberto, an elderly singer recognised as an authority within this tradition.

    The project explores how to construct a portrait of a singer using sound alone. Conversations, domestic surroundings, arrivals, greetings, collective singing and individual voices are brought together to show that someone does not become audible as a singer in isolation. His presence emerges through the family, community and ritual relationships that sustain the practice.

    Narrowing an archive in order to begin listening

    The collaboration arose after several conversations in which Javiera told me about the many recordings she had made with a TASCAM recorder during her fieldwork. I told her about my experience working with audio and showed her Metagenome. We later met at her home to review some of the material.

    The size of the archive made it difficult to decide where to begin. I proposed concentrating on the recordings from a single vigilia—an overnight gathering centred on collective devotional singing—rather than immediately attempting to organise or represent the collection as a whole. The archive’s broader classification required a separate archival process, for which Javiera has experience in community archiving and contextual knowledge that I do not possess.

    Javiera selected Don Gilberto’s vigilia. Her choice reflected his recognition as a singer, his advanced age and her wish to create something that could be dedicated to him.

    Formulating a question through editing

    At the outset, the question had not yet taken a definitive form. In our conversations, we explored several possibilities: what does canto a lo divino sound like; how does a singer sound; who is a singer when approached through sound; and which elements of this practice can be made perceptible without images?

    My participation focused on honing these questions and translating them into a conceptual and narrative direction. The problem ceased to be simply selecting representative recordings and became one of constructing a form of listening capable of showing how a person comes to be recognised as a singer within a network of relationships.

    The title Retrato familiar expresses that orientation. The piece does not seek to isolate an individual voice or produce an exhaustive biography, but to approach Don Gilberto through the sonic world that surrounds him and helps sustain his practice.

    Working through listening together

    The first stage took place at Javiera’s home. As we reviewed the recordings, I pointed out editing possibilities, showed her the operations available in the software, and documented her reactions to different fragments.

    This joint work allowed us to recognise scenes, voices, and relationships that I could not have interpreted without her knowledge of the field. At the same time, listening through the software opened new possibilities for ordering the material, juxtaposing moments, and trying out a structure.

    Javiera later sent me a digital copy of the project and I continued working independently. Our collaboration became iterative. I would prepare a version, we would meet to listen to it, Javiera would provide feedback and we would try out preliminary changes. I would then refine those changes at home so that they could be integrated without overly abrupt transitions.

    Building relationships through editing

    I made the technical editing and mixing decisions in GarageBand. The work included selecting and trimming excerpts, rearranging material, creating fades, automating volume, panning, equalising, adjusting levels and constructing transitions.

    These operations did not function solely as technical corrections. Cutting, bringing sounds together or separating them altered the relationships that could be heard between people, spaces and songs. Editing thus became a way of exploring the archive and proposing an interpretation of what sustains the figure of a singer.

    The structure moves from the sounds of the house and the participants’ arrival towards greetings, conversations, collective singing and Don Gilberto’s more distinct emergence. This progression seeks to avoid separating his voice from the relationships that give it context.

    Status and scope

    A draft that remains open

    Current status

    The current version is an advanced draft, estimated to be approximately sixty per cent complete. Its structure and conceptual direction are already defined, but the piece is not yet finished.

    Completion depends on additional recordings that Javiera agreed to select and send. These materials will make it possible to complete the final section and review the overall balance of the piece. A final round of joint editing, mixing and listening will then be required.

    The version published at this stage documents an ongoing collaborative process; it is neither a finished work nor the definitive version of the piece.

    Scope

    Retrato familiar does not seek to represent canto a lo divino in its entirety or replace the ethnographic work from which the archive emerged. Nor does it present the edited piece as a transparent reproduction of the vigilia.

    The piece offers a partial interpretation constructed through selection and editing. Its question is more specific: how can someone be made audible as a singer without separating his voice from the family, community and ritual relationships that make that recognition possible?

    Authorship, research and responsibilities

    The research, fieldwork, recordings and ethnographic knowledge of the context belong to Javiera Montecinos. She selected Don Gilberto’s vigilia, identified people and situations, contextualised the recordings and validated the narrative decisions through her knowledge of the field.

    I proposed initially narrowing the archive to a single vigilia, played a central role in formulating the anthropological question and developed the conceptual direction of the piece. I also selected the material together with Javiera and was responsible for all technical editing and mixing decisions.

    The successive versions were reviewed and approved jointly. Javiera authorised the publication of the draft in the portfolio and holds the informed consents required to use the voices, singing and recordings it incorporates.
